# QuoteCraft — from RFQ to bid

A team of model-directed agents that reads a tender across four business websites it has never seen, works out the
bid the rules call for, and enters and signs it in the tender portal.

## How it works

```
task brief ──► model reads it: tender, scenario date, authorized senders
                    │
   ┌────────────────┼──────────────────┬─────────────────┐
   ▼                ▼                  ▼                 ▼
 agent            agent              agent             agent        one per website, each in its own browser:
 tender portal    supplier portal    ERP               webmail      the model picks every click, search and page
   │  keep          │  keep            │  keep           │  keep
   └────────────────┴───────┬──────────┴─────────────────┘
                            ▼
                     shared case file        a model call turns each filed page into typed facts;
                            │                the brief's rules yield the open questions all agents see
                            ▼
                      calculator.py          the bid rules as exact Decimal arithmetic
                            ▼
                     submission agent        fills the bid form it finds; the mail agent fetches the TAN
```

1. **Read the brief.** One model call extracts the tender reference, the scenario date, the bidder and which
   mailbox the rules authorize for which kind of record.
2. **Investigate in parallel.** One agent per website (`worker.Agent`). Each turn it sees its page as accessible
   text with numbered controls (`browser_env.Tab`), plus the case file and its open questions, and answers with
   actions: log in, click, fill, select, search, page through a list, download a file, or `keep` the page as
   evidence. Nothing in the code knows a URL, a selector or a click path of any website.
3. **File facts.** `keep` hands the page to a second model call that extracts typed records (positions, Q&A
   answers, revisions, requirements, materials, price conditions, mail records). `casefile.CaseFile` merges them
   and derives what is still unknown: a catalogue group found in the specification becomes an ERP question, a key
   in a Q&A answer becomes a mailbox question, and so on. Agents finish when their website has nothing left to add.
4. **Calculate.** `calculator.calculate_bid` applies the bid rules of the brief: latest clarification, withdrawn
   answers, scoped amendments, usable travel, sets to pieces, price scales, FX, conditional discount, condition
   clauses, shared stock, delivery commitments, cartons, pooled setup, project bonus, rounding. A position that
   lacks evidence is left out rather than guessed.
5. **Submit.** `submit.submit_bid` gives the bid to an agent on the tender portal, which fills whatever bid form
   it finds, asks a mail agent for the signing TAN and confirms the receipt.

## What is model and what is code

| The model decides | Code does |
| --- | --- |
| where to go, what to search for, which record or document matters | renders the page, carries out the chosen action |
| how to pass a popup, access check, login or error page | retries a server error, re-reads the page |
| which page is evidence and of what kind | pages through a list the model chose, reads a file it chose |
| what a page says (extraction into typed facts) | parses numbers and dates, checks sender, reference and date |
| when a search is complete or a record does not exist | arithmetic, rounding, allocation |
| how to fill and sign the bid form | — |

No scenario value (reference, material, price, key, login, TAN) appears anywhere in the package.

## Files

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `agent.py` | Entry point: reads the run, starts the site agents, calculates, hands the bid to the submission agent |
| `worker.py` | The agent loop: page text in, the model's actions out |
| `browser_env.py` | A tab as accessible text (labels, descriptions, tooltips, frames, collapsed sections) and the actions on it |
| `casefile.py` | Evidence to typed facts, open questions, calculator inputs |
| `calculator.py` | The bid rules as Decimal arithmetic |
| `submit.py` | Bid entry and signing |
| `llm.py` | The hosted Qwen through the run's metering proxy: JSON replies, retries, a concurrency cap |
| `run.py`, `browsers.py`, `models.py` | The starter kit's plumbing: the run contract, the run's browsers, the hosted models |
| `agent.json` | Setup (`uv sync`), run command, four browsers, the hosted `qwen` |
| `tests/` | The calculator rule by rule, the page rendering against local fixtures, the plumbing against fakes |

## Running it

In the sandbox the platform sets everything (`CHALLENGE_API_URL`, `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`, `CDP_URLS`, `QWEN_*`):

```sh
atira test-run . --challenge rfq
```

On your machine, against the public websites with the scouting logins (nothing counts), with `atira models proxy`
running in another terminal:

```sh
python ../tools/local_run.py --no-submit
```

Switches: `AGENT_SKIP_SUBMIT=1` stops before the bid form, `AGENT_SITES=a,b` starts only those site agents,
`AGENT_MAX_STEPS` caps an agent's turns, `AGENT_DUMP=<file>` writes the case file as JSON.

```sh
uv run python -m unittest discover tests
```

| where to go, what to search for, which record or document matters | renders the page, carries out the chosen action |
| how to pass a popup, access check, login or error page | retries a server error, re-reads the page |
| which page is evidence and of what kind | pages through a list the model chose, reads a file it chose |
| what a page says (extraction into typed facts) | parses numbers and dates, checks sender, reference and date |
| when a search is complete or a record does not exist | arithmetic, rounding, allocation |
| how to fill and sign the bid form | — |

No scenario value (reference, material, price, key, login, TAN) appears anywhere in the package.

## Files

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `agent.py` | Entry point: reads the run, starts the site agents, calculates, hands the bid to the submission agent |
| `worker.py` | The agent loop: page text in, the model's actions out |
| `browser_env.py` | A tab as accessible text (labels, descriptions, tooltips, frames, collapsed sections) and the actions on it |
| `casefile.py` | Evidence to typed facts, open questions, calculator inputs |
| `calculator.py` | The bid rules as Decimal arithmetic |
| `submit.py` | Bid entry and signing |
| `llm.py` | The hosted Qwen through the run's metering proxy: JSON replies, retries, a concurrency cap |
| `run.py`, `browsers.py`, `models.py` | The starter kit's plumbing: the run contract, the run's browsers, the hosted models |
| `agent.json` | Setup (`uv sync`), run command, four browsers, the hosted `qwen` |
| `tests/` | The calculator rule by rule, the page rendering against local fixtures, the plumbing against fakes |

## Running it

In the sandbox the platform sets everything (`CHALLENGE_API_URL`, `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`, `CDP_URLS`, `QWEN_*`):

```sh
atira test-run . --challenge rfq
```

On your machine, against the public websites with the scouting logins (nothing counts), with `atira models proxy`
running in another terminal:

```sh
python ../tools/local_run.py --no-submit
```

Switches: `AGENT_SKIP_SUBMIT=1` stops before the bid form, `AGENT_SITES=a,b` starts only those site agents,
`AGENT_MAX_STEPS` caps an agent's turns, `AGENT_DUMP=<file>` writes the case file as JSON.

```sh
uv run python -m unittest discover tests
```

"""The bid-entry stage against a scripted model and fake tabs: what the clerk is told, how the signing code travels
from the mailbox agent to the clerk, and what `submit_bid` reports."""
import sys
import time
import unittest
from decimal import Decimal
from pathlib import Path
from types import SimpleNamespace
from unittest.mock import patch

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))

import llm  # noqa: E402
import submit  # noqa: E402
from calculator import Bid, Line, Material  # noqa: E402

CONTEXT = {"tender_reference": "T-0001", "scenario_date": "2030-03-01T09:00:00+00:00", "company": "Example Works",
           "vat_id": "XX000000001", "email": "sales@bidder.example"}


def a_bid(**changes) -> Bid:
    material = Material(number="M-1", bore_mm=50, stroke_mm=200, pressure_bar=160, mounting="flange",
                        certification="none")
    priced = Line("1", "M-1", 40, unit_price=Decimal("12.50"), lead_time_weeks=3, base_unit_price=Decimal("12.00"),
                  surcharge_per_unit=Decimal("0.50"), packaging_per_unit=Decimal("0"), rebate_total=None,
                  material=material)
    bid = Bid("T-0001", "bid", Decimal("2.5"), [priced], Decimal("500.00"), omitted=["2"])
    for name, value in changes.items():
        setattr(bid, name, value)
    return bid


class FakeTab:
    """As much of a Tab as the agent loop touches; it records the actions it was given."""

    def __init__(self, site_id: str, view: str | None = None):
        self.site_id, self.base_url = site_id, f"http://{site_id}.test"
        self.page = SimpleNamespace(url=self.base_url + "/start", main_frame=self)
        self.document, self.document_source, self.done = "", "", []
        self.view = view or f"url: {self.page.url}\ntitle: {self.site_id}\n[1] button \"go\""

    async def evaluate(self, script):
        return True

    async def observe(self) -> str:
        return self.view

    def take_events(self) -> list[str]:
        return []

    async def click(self, aid) -> str:
        self.done.append(("click", aid))
        return f"clicked [{aid}]"

    async def fill(self, aid, text, enter=False) -> str:
        self.done.append(("fill", aid, text))
        return f"filled [{aid}]"


class Script:
    """Stands in for llm.chat_json: answers each agent, named by `label`, with its next scripted reply."""

    def __init__(self, **replies):
        self.replies, self.asked = replies, []

    async def __call__(self, messages, *, think=True, max_tokens=6000, label=""):
        self.asked.append({"label": label, "think": think, "system": messages[0]["content"],
                           "user": messages[-1]["content"]})
        return self.replies[label].pop(0) if self.replies.get(label) else {}

    def turns(self, label: str) -> list[dict]:
        return [call for call in self.asked if call["label"] == label]


def done(**fields) -> dict:
    return {"thought": "", "actions": [{"do": "done", **fields}]}


class TheBidSheet(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_amounts_are_exact_text_and_unknown_values_stay_empty(self):
        sheet = submit.bid_sheet(a_bid())
        line = sheet["positions"][0]
        self.assertEqual((line["unit_price"], line["base_unit_price"], line["surcharge_per_unit"]),
                         ("12.50", "12.00", "0.50"))
        self.assertEqual(line["packaging_per_unit"], "0.00")  # a known zero is entered
        self.assertIsNone(line["rebate_total"])  # an unknown value is left blank
        self.assertEqual((line["quantity"], line["lead_time_weeks"]), (40, 3))
        self.assertEqual((sheet["total_net"], sheet["discount_percent"], sheet["omitted_positions"]),
                         ("500.00", 2.5, ["2"]))

    def test_each_position_carries_the_offered_materials_attributes(self):
        material = submit.bid_sheet(a_bid())["positions"][0]["material"]
        self.assertEqual(material, {"bore_mm": 50, "stroke_mm": 200, "pressure_bar": 160, "mounting": "flange",
                                    "certification": "none"})

    def test_a_no_bid_is_an_empty_sheet_with_a_whole_number_discount(self):
        sheet = submit.bid_sheet(a_bid(decision="no_bid", lines=[], omitted=[], total_net=Decimal("0"),
                                       discount_percent=Decimal("0")))
        self.assertEqual((sheet["decision"], sheet["positions"], sheet["total_net"], sheet["discount_percent"]),
                         ("no_bid", [], "0.00", 0))


class EnteringTheBid(unittest.IsolatedAsyncioTestCase):
    async def run_with(self, script: Script, mail_tab="mail", seconds: float = 900) -> tuple[dict, FakeTab]:
        tender = FakeTab("tender")
        mail = FakeTab("mail") if mail_tab else None
        with patch.object(llm, "chat_json", script):
            result = await submit.submit_bid(tender, mail, a_bid(), CONTEXT, "THE BRIEF", time.time() + seconds)
        return result, tender

    async def test_the_clerk_is_given_the_brief_the_bidder_and_the_sheet(self):
        script = Script(submit=[done(answer="R-1")])
        await self.run_with(script)
        first = script.turns("submit")[0]
        for expected in ("THE BRIEF", "Example Works", "XX000000001", "sales@bidder.example", '"unit_price": "12.50"',
                         '"omitted_positions"', "ask_mail", "http://tender.test"):
            self.assertIn(expected, first["system"])
        self.assertIn("tender T-0001", first["user"])
        self.assertNotIn("TIME IS SHORT", first["user"])

    async def test_the_signing_code_comes_from_an_agent_on_the_mailbox(self):
        script = Script(
            submit=[{"thought": "", "actions": [{"do": "ask_mail", "task": "the code I requested just now"}]},
                    {"thought": "", "actions": [{"do": "fill", "id": 1, "text": "CODE-7"}, {"do": "click", "id": 1}]},
                    done(answer="R-1", summary="received")],
            courier=[done(answer=" CODE-7 ")])
        result, tender = await self.run_with(script)
        courier = script.turns("courier")[0]
        self.assertIn("http://mail.test", courier["system"])
        self.assertIn("T-0001", courier["system"])
        self.assertIn("the code I requested just now", courier["user"])
        self.assertIn('the mailbox colleague answers: "CODE-7"', script.turns("submit")[1]["user"])
        self.assertIn(("fill", 1, "CODE-7"), tender.done)
        self.assertEqual(result, {"submitted": True, "receipt": "R-1", "notes": "received"})

    async def test_a_code_that_was_handed_out_is_not_handed_out_again(self):
        ask = {"thought": "", "actions": [{"do": "ask_mail", "task": "a fresh code"}]}
        script = Script(submit=[ask, ask, done(answer="R-1")], courier=[done(answer="CODE-1"), done(answer="CODE-2")])
        await self.run_with(script)
        first, second = script.turns("courier")
        self.assertNotIn("CODE-1", first["user"])
        self.assertIn("- CODE-1", second["user"])
        self.assertIn("Codes from the mailbox so far, oldest first: CODE-1, CODE-2", script.turns("submit")[2]["user"])

    async def test_the_clerk_hears_when_the_mailbox_has_nothing(self):
        ask = {"thought": "", "actions": [{"do": "ask_mail", "task": "the code"}]}
        script = Script(submit=[ask, done(summary="no code")], courier=[done(summary="no such message")])
        result, _ = await self.run_with(script)
        self.assertIn("the mailbox colleague found nothing: no such message", script.turns("submit")[1]["user"])
        self.assertEqual(result, {"submitted": False, "receipt": "", "notes": "no code"})

    async def test_without_a_mailbox_in_the_run_the_clerk_is_told_so(self):
        ask = {"thought": "", "actions": [{"do": "ask_mail", "task": "the code"}]}
        script = Script(submit=[ask, done(summary="cannot sign")])
        result, _ = await self.run_with(script, mail_tab=None)
        self.assertIn("there is no mailbox in this run", script.turns("submit")[1]["user"])
        self.assertEqual(script.turns("courier"), [])
        self.assertFalse(result["submitted"])

    async def test_a_bid_without_confirmation_is_not_reported_as_submitted(self):
        result, _ = await self.run_with(Script(submit=[]))  # the model never gives a usable reply

item.stdout:
Usage: atira test-run <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]

Pack <dir>, run it once in the sandbox on the public data and open its run page; --follow prints its place in the queue, then streams its logs here
Atira Challenges CLI

Usage: atira <command> [options]   (or: node atira.mjs <command> [options])

Commands:
  login [--device] [--key <key>]
      Sign in through the browser (--device: with a code instead) and store a personal token, mode 0600; --key stores a team key where there is no GitHub sign-in
  logout
      Revoke the stored token on the server and forget it
  whoami
      Show who you are signed in as, your team and when the token expires
  token
      Print the token in use, for curl: curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)" ...
  upgrade
      Download the server's current CLI, check its SHA-256 and replace this file
  challenges
      List the challenges
  challenge <id>
      Print a challenge as Markdown: task, websites, rules, run contract, submitting, answer schema
  scout [--challenge <id>] [--env [--port <port>]]
      Print the published scouting logins for the public websites; --env prints shell exports (CHALLENGE_SCOUTING, CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS, each site's URL, and QWEN_BASE_URL, QWEN_API_KEY, CLEF_BASE_URL, CLEF_API_KEY pointed at atira models proxy) to run your agent locally against them
  models proxy [--port <port>]
      Run a local proxy on 127.0.0.1 (port 8765) to the free models, QWEN_BASE_URL and CLEF_BASE_URL: it prints the exports
  test-run <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]
      Pack <dir>, run it once in the sandbox on the public data and open its run page; --follow prints its place in the queue, then streams its logs here
  submit <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]
      Pack <dir> and submit it for a ranked run, public and final: review, then one scored run on the public dataset; opens the team page, which follows both; --follow prints the review, each run's place in the queue and its end here
  final [--best-of <1|3>] [--challenge <id>]
      Choose one final attempt or best of three before the final run starts; your own model keys cost up to 3×
  status [<id>] [--challenge <id>]
      Your latest submissions and test runs, or one submission (sub_), test run (reh_) or run (run_)
  logs <run> [--follow]
      Print a test or scored run's logs; --follow polls until the run has ended
  package <id> [--out <dir>]
      Show the package a test run (reh_ or run_), scored run or submission (sub_) of your team used, as uploaded: agent.json and each file's size; --out saves the .tar.gz in <dir>
  cancel <run>
      Cancel a test or scored run that has not finished: its sandbox is removed and the run fails
  leaderboard [--challenge <id>]
      Print the leaderboard
  mcp
      Serve MCP on stdio, so a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, ...) can list and debug your runs: why a run failed, logs by time, model calls, where the time went, a browser's screen at a time, recorded inputs, two runs compared, the package a run used; it can start and wait for test runs, and cancel a run or submit when you confirm

Options:
  --challenge, -c <id>  The challenge (default: ATIRA_CHALLENGE, else the platform's first)
  --json                Machine-readable output on stdout, errors included
  --help, -h            This help, or a command's (also: atira help <command>)
  --version, -v         This file's SHA-256, as install.sh printed it, and Node's version

Environment:
  ATIRA_API             The platform (default: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai)
  ATIRA_TOKEN           A token to use instead of the one `login` stored
  ATIRA_CHALLENGE       The default challenge
  ATIRA_BROWSER         The command that opens pages (login, test-run, submit), or none to only print links

Exit codes:
  0 done   1 network or server error   2 usage   3 not signed in, or the credential was refused   4 not found
  5 invalid request or package   6 busy: a submission still in evaluation, three test runs already waiting, a rate limit, or a run that already finished
  7 the run failed or timed out (logs --follow, test-run --follow), or the submission did not complete (submit --follow)

content.text: what strategy are we using?
what strategy are we using?

We use a four-stage, model-directed strategy:

1. Investigate in parallel  
   Four browser agents explore the tender portal, supplier portal, ERP, and email separately. Each agent chooses its own navigation, searches, and documents based on what it sees.

2. Build a shared evidence case file  
   Relevant pages are saved as typed facts—positions, requirements, materials, conditions, clarifications, and mail records—with their source/provenance attached.

3. Calculate deterministically  
   The calculator applies the commercial rules using exact `Decimal` arithmetic: pricing, discounts, currency, quantities, lead times, packaging, stock, and the other bid rules.

4. Complete and safeguard submission  
   A final portal agent fills the discovered bid form, retrieves the TAN from mail, handles recoverable issues, and uses a live pre-submit checklist before the final confirmation.

The key idea is: model for understanding and adapting to changing portals; deterministic code for calculations and safety checks.

Winning Strategy for Autonomous RFQ Extraction and Navigation on Unseen Web Environments
The Evaluation Environment and Industrial RFQ Complexity
The deployment of autonomous agents across unseen web environments constitutes one of the most rigorous frontiers in applied artificial intelligence. In the industrial software sector, companies such as Atira build commercial orchestration platforms designed to automate the end-to-end processing of complex requests for quotation (RFQs), engineering tenders, and supplier questionnaires. Industrial tenders routinely span hundreds of clauses, referencing precise technical tolerances, regulatory standards such as DIN and ISO norms, and cross-departmental commercial obligations. When evaluating machine intelligence against these workflows, benchmark organizers construct environments that mirror the heterogeneity of industrial procurement portals: non-standard design systems, dynamic JavaScript frameworks, complex multi-step forms, nested tables, and authentication boundaries.   

Autonomous web agents evaluated on held-out or unseen websites face acute failure rates. Standard robotic process automation (RPA) workflows rely on static XPath identifiers or brittle CSS selectors; across dynamic enterprise portals, minor DOM mutations trigger script breakages in 30% to 50% of automated runs. Conversely, naive Large Language Model (LLM) agents that ingest full, unpruned HTML documents rapidly saturate model context windows with irrelevant layout wrappers and styling tokens, resulting in severe grounding confusion, high inference latency, and elevated hallucination rates.   

Excelling in an evaluation regime characterized by unseen target sites requires an architecture that discards assumptions of structural familiarity. The system must possess universal perceptual grounding, strict modularity between planning and execution, and test-time verification loops capable of intercepting execution drift before errors compound.   

Comparative Analysis of Autonomous Web Perception Frameworks
The fundamental determinant of zero-shot transfer across unfamiliar web pages is the fidelity and compression ratio of the perceptual representation supplied to the reasoning model. The agent must reconstruct page semantics and interactive affordances without ingesting irrelevant DOM noise.   

Observation Paradigm	Latency per Step	Mean Context Cost	Grounding Precision	Zero-Shot Transfer to Unseen Layouts	Primary Failure Mechanisms
Raw HTML Injection	Low	40k–100k+ tokens	Low	Very Low	
Context window truncation, class obfuscation, CSS/SVG clutter

Pure Vision (Screenshot / GUI)	High	1.5k–3k tokens	Moderate	Moderate to High	
Resolution scaling errors, coordinate drift, off-screen blindness

Accessibility Tree (AX-Tree)	Very Low	2k–8k tokens	High	High	
Canvas element omission, visual layering and z-index blindness

Hybrid (Pruned AX-Tree + Set-of-Marks)	Moderate	4k–10k tokens	Highest	Highest	
Minor latency overhead during selective visual fallback calls

  
The browser's accessibility tree provides a standardized structural hierarchy originally designed for assistive technologies, stripping presentational tags such as nested division wrappers while retaining semantic roles, accessible names, values, and interactive states. In production web applications, raw DOM representations frequently exceed 100,000 tokens, whereas a distilled accessibility tree captures identical operational semantics within 3,000 to 8,000 tokens. Furthermore, accessibility trees normalize heterogeneous implementations; an interactive trigger is parsed consistently as an actionable element regardless of whether it was authored as an anchor tag, a native button, or an ARIA-labeled span.   

Despite these structural benefits, exclusive reliance on accessibility trees exposes agents to visual blind spots. Custom canvas controls, dynamic file upload drop zones, floating modal backdrops, and complex geospatial interfaces frequently omit ARIA labels or fail to register interactive roles. To resolve these limitations, modern architectures employ a hybrid perception stack that relies on the pruned accessibility tree as the primary input and activates Set-of-Marks (SoM) visual overlays selectively.   

Under the Set-of-Marks methodology, interactive elements are bounded using client-side JavaScript, and high-contrast numerical badges are painted over the rendered page screenshot. When an element fails to reveal clear semantic metadata in the accessibility tree, the multimodal backbone references the visual badge ID directly, establishing dual-channel grounding across both structural and visual modalities.   

Hierarchical Multi-Agent Decoupling: Planner, Actor, Validator, Extractor
Monolithic architectures—in which a single prompt is tasked with simultaneous navigation planning, DOM parsing, coordinate localization, and structured field extraction—exhibit steep degradation over long-horizon tasks on unfamiliar websites. As operational trajectories lengthen, context pollution obscures critical instructions, leading to missed form validations and navigational loops. Top-performing agents decouple these responsibilities into specialized, asynchronous roles within a coordinated agentic loop.   

Functional Role	Primary Input Data	Permitted Action Space	Quality Control & Verification Mechanism
Strategic Planner	Global Task Objective, Milestone Trace, Historical Context	decompose_subgoal(), replan(), terminate_task()	
Tracks milestone progression; prevents navigational deviation

Interactive Actor	Active AX-Tree Snapshot, Current Subgoal, Last Error Trace	click(ref), type(ref, text), select(ref, val), scroll(dir)	
Validates element existence and interactivity before dispatch

State Validator / Critic	Pre-Action AX Hash, Post-Action AX Hash, URL Trace	confirm_transition(), trigger_recovery(), flag_loop()	
Computes structural DOM differences; confirms state mutation

Schema-Guided Extractor	Rendered Page Buffer, Intercepted Payloads, Target Schema	extract_payload(), validate_types(), flag_discrepancy()	
Validates extraction completeness against strict Pydantic schemas

  
The Strategic Planner maintains the overarching execution blueprint without handling raw DOM elements or immediate button targets. It operates over abstract subgoals, such as locating the RFQ portal, querying catalog specifications, downloading tender documentation, and completing commercial registration forms. The Planner updates its state only upon the verified completion or confirmed failure of a milestone, shielding its context from the transient operational noise of page scrolling and intermediate keystrokes.   

The Interactive Actor operates strictly within the boundary of an immediate subgoal. Its input is restricted to the current active accessibility tree snapshot, indexed with dynamic numerical references (ref=N), and the single atomic instruction supplied by the Planner. By discarding previous dialogue turns and preserving only the latest page snapshot, the Actor consumes a constant token budget per step, preventing token exhaustion and attention dilution across extensive navigation sequences.   

The State Validator acts as an execution critic that runs immediately after each browser dispatch. Autonomous agents frequently assume that an emitted action achieved its desired effect; however, web forms frequently reject input silently due to validation errors, network throttling, or overlapping modal backdrops. The Validator computes structural differences between pre-action and post-action page states. If an Actor issues a click event on a submission button but the URL remains invariant and no subsequent modal or DOM mutation appears, the Validator flags the event as unfulfilled and injects targeted diagnostic context back into the Actor's operational prompt.   

The Schema-Guided Extractor specializes in turning unstructured web text and tabular layouts into validated data models. When evaluating industrial RFQ sites, information extraction requires strict normalization across mechanical tolerances, engineering standards, currency codes, and delivery schedules. The Extractor applies Pydantic type constraints and regular expression rules to ensure that all extracted tender entities conform to technical validation criteria before being submitted to the final scoring harness.   

Deterministic Edge-Case Engineering and Failure Mitigation
Operating across unseen web portals exposes automated agents to recurring failure modes that cannot be solved purely through prompt modification. A competitive system must incorporate deterministic software wrappers that enforce stability at the browser runtime layer.   

Navigational loops—commonly termed doom-loops—occur when an agent repeatedly executes an ineffective action, such as clicking a non-responsive element or toggling between identical tabs. The runtime mitigates this failure mode by maintaining a rolling registry of structural state hashes computed directly over pruned accessibility snapshots:

The circuit breaker temporarily revokes the Actor's primary action proposal, forces an exploratory action—such as vertical viewport scrolling or navigating back one level in the browser history—and alerts the Planner to formulate an alternate navigational branch.   

Unseen modern websites frequently introduce non-deterministic modal dialogs, cookie consent banners, and shadow DOM elements that obscure interactive components and intercept user events. The automation layer resolves these layout hurdles through three programmatic interventions:   

First, the Playwright harness executes an automated consent dismissal script prior to handing execution to the perception layer, identifying common CMP attributes matching patterns such as button:has-text("Accept") or [aria-label*="cookie"].   

Second, the locator engine leverages deep CSS selectors that pierce open shadow roots automatically, ensuring that web components authored within custom shadow boundaries remain fully indexed in the accessibility snapshot.

Third, every click interaction is preceded by an explicit scroll-into-view command combined with pointer-event verification, ensuring that sticky headers or floating banners do not absorb clicks intended for underlying target fields.

A critical competitive advantage on industrial data portals involves bypassing the visual interface entirely when extracting dense, paginated tables. Many modern enterprise RFQ systems fetch tabular technical specifications via background XHR or Fetch requests returning JSON payloads. By binding an asynchronous response listener to the Playwright browser context, the agent inspects incoming HTTP network streams:   

Python
# Asynchronous interception of tabular RFQ network responses
def attach_network_sniffer(page, captured_buffers):
    def handle_response(response):
        content_type = response.headers.get("content-type", "")
        if "application/json" in content_type or "text/csv" in content_type:
            try:
                payload = response.json()
                if any(k in str(payload).lower() for k in ["spec", "rfq", "tender", "parts", "tolerance"]):
                    captured_buffers.append(payload)
            except Exception:
                pass
    page.on("response", handle_response)
When an agent lands on a complex data grid containing multiple pages of line items, it checks the captured network buffer before executing manual, step-by-step UI pagination. If the underlying REST endpoint returns the complete, unpaginated dataset in a single JSON payload, the agent routes the raw network data directly to the Schema Extractor, eliminating multiple slow, error-prone visual navigation steps.   

Architectural Implementation Blueprint
The end-to-end framework operates as a closed-loop system connecting the headless browser, the hybrid perception module, the hierarchical agent core, and the schema extraction engine. The browser harness establishes the runtime environment, suppresses automated detection flags, and collects network payloads. The perception layer distills the active DOM into a numbered, pruned accessibility snapshot, falling back to Set-of-Marks visual tagging if semantic roles are missing.   

The Planner evaluates the active task milestone against this processed page view and supplies a concise instruction to the Actor. The Actor selects a target reference ID and an action primitive, which the browser executes. The Validator immediately computes the post-action state delta; upon confirming a valid transition, execution advances to the next step, while an invariant state triggers the loop-prevention circuit breaker. Finally, when navigation reaches the relevant data views, the Schema Extractor parses the content into validated structured output.   

JavaScript
// In-browser JavaScript function to generate distilled, indexed accessibility trees
function generatePrunedAccessibilitySnapshot() {
  const targetRoles = new Set([
    'button', 'link', 'textbox', 'checkbox', 'radio', 
    'combobox', 'menuitem', 'tab', 'switch', 'treeitem'
  ]);
  
  let referenceId = 1;
  const elements = [];
  const treeWalker = document.createTreeWalker(document.body, NodeFilter.SHOW_ELEMENT);

  while (treeWalker.nextNode()) {
    const node = treeWalker.currentNode;
    const computed = window.getComputedStyle(node);
    if (computed.display === 'none' || computed.visibility === 'hidden' || computed.opacity === '0') {
      continue;
    }

    const assignedRole = node.getAttribute('role') || node.tagName.toLowerCase();
    const isInteractive = targetRoles.has(assignedRole) || 
                          node.tagName === 'INPUT' || 
                          node.tagName === 'BUTTON' || 
                          node.tagName === 'SELECT' || 
                          node.onclick !== null || 
                          computed.cursor === 'pointer';

    if (isInteractive) {
      node.setAttribute('data-agent-ref', referenceId.toString());
      elements.push({
        ref: referenceId,
        role: assignedRole,
        label: (node.innerText || node.getAttribute('aria-label') || node.getAttribute('placeholder') || '').trim().slice(0, 100),
        value: node.value || '',
        tag: node.tagName.toLowerCase(),
        disabled: node.disabled || node.getAttribute('aria-disabled') === 'true'
      });
      referenceId++;
    }
  }
  return elements;
}

import hashlib
from typing import Optional, List
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class AtomicAction(BaseModel):
    action: str = Field(description="Action primitive: click, fill, select, scroll, wait, complete")
    ref: Optional[int] = Field(default=None, description="Target numerical reference ID from snapshot")
    text: Optional[str] = Field(default="", description="Input text string for fill action")
    rationale: str = Field(description="Operational reasoning justifying the primitive selection")

Standard robotic process automation (RPA) workflows rely on static XPath identifiers or brittle CSS selectors; across dynamic enterprise portals, minor DOM mutations trigger script breakages in 30% to 50% of automated runs. Conversely, naive Large Language Model (LLM) agents that ingest full, unpruned HTML documents rapidly saturate model context windows with irrelevant layout wrappers and styling tokens, resulting in severe grounding confusion, high inference latency, and elevated hallucination rates.

The system must possess universal perceptual grounding, strict modularity between planning and execution, and test-time verification loops capable of intercepting execution drift before errors compound.

# From RFQ to bid

**Turn a public tender into a correct, signed bid without a person touching it.**

You work for a German hydraulics manufacturer that wants to bid on a public tender for hydraulic cylinders. What you need is spread over four websites: the tender portal, a supplier portal with the buyer's specification, your company's ERP and the sales inbox. They behave like real business software, with logins, popups, session timeouts and outdated documents. Your agent reads all of it, applies the bid rules and enters one priced, signed bid in the tender portal.

**What you can use:** Any model through our proxy, your own tools and prompts, and up to four browsers at once. A model does the work in the sandbox: it finds its way through the websites and makes the decisions during the run. No fixed scripts, no crawlers, no copied values, no person helping.

**How you win:** Your bid has to be eligible first. After that, the most accurate bid wins, and between equally accurate bids, the cheaper and faster one. The leaderboard uses the public data. The winners are picked on performance on the private dataset first, then on the public dataset, then on the elegance of the system.

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Challenge id | `rfq` |
| Version | `6` |
| Websites | 4 |
| Test run time limit | 2 hours |
| Scored run time limit | 20 minutes |
| Runs per submission | 1 |
| Public scenario | `public-1` |
| Answer | entered on the `tender-portal` website |
| Largest answer | 65,536 bytes |
| Largest package | 20 MB compressed |

Web page: [https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq) · Leaderboard: [Markdown](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md) · Getting started: [Markdown](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/start.md) · For agents: [llms.txt](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/llms.txt) · [OpenAPI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/openapi.json) · [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md) · [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md)

## Quick start for agents

Set the platform URL, install the CLI and sign in once: `atira login` opens the browser, where you approve a personal token for this device (`atira login --device` prints a link and a code instead, for a machine without a browser; plain curl uses the [device flow](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#signing-in)). Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header, or as `Authorization: Bearer`.

```sh
export ATIRA_API=https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai
curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | sh   # the CLI for Node 24; read it first: curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | less
# or without installing: curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/cli.mjs" -o atira.mjs && node atira.mjs --help
atira login   # approve in the browser
export ATIRA_TOKEN=$(atira token)   # for curl
eval "$(atira scout --challenge rfq --env)"   # logins for the public websites, to run your agent locally
atira test-run ./my-agent --challenge rfq   # one sandbox run on the public dataset, opened live
atira submit ./my-agent --challenge rfq     # review, then the scored run on the public dataset
atira status
```

## The task

One tender, four German websites, one bid.

The agent produces: **One bid**. It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.

## The websites

Each run gets its own logins, in the run's `access`. To look around yourself, use the scouting logins below. Expect what real business software throws at you: popups, session timeouts, outdated documents and look-alike records. Everything your agent needs fits on a 1280×800 screen.

### 1. Tender portal (Vergabeportal, `tender-portal`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-tender-portal.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: The public tender, its bill of quantities, the bidder Q&A that changes quantities, and the bid configurator.
- What makes it hard: Cookie wall, flaky error pages, documents behind an expression of interest, iframes and ZIP files, a deadline in another timezone.

### 2. Supplier portal (Lieferantenportal, `customer-portal`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-customer-portal.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: The buyer's technical specification and its revisions.
- What makes it hard: Opens the oldest revision first, nested document viewers, paged requirement tables.

### 3. ERP (`erp`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-erp.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: Your company's materials, stock, lead times and price conditions with validity periods and quantity scales.
- What makes it hard: SAP-style transaction codes, an F4 search popup, status codes, a short session timeout.

### 4. Webmail (Werkpost, `mail`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-mail.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: Your sales inbox, with the sales director's discount approval and the signing TAN.
- What makes it hard: Look-alike approvals for other tenders, superseded approvals, an archive folder, paging.

## Public and private data

There are two datasets. The leaderboard uses the public one, on these websites. The final run uses a private dataset: the same jobs, bid rules and answer format, on different websites with other content and data. We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order: performance on the private dataset, performance on the public dataset, and the elegance of the system.

- **Public dataset:** The leaderboard uses the public dataset (public-1), the websites and data you scout and test on. Each submission runs once on it. We don't publish the correct answer. Test runs and the scouting logins use it too.
- **Private dataset (the final run):** When the hackathon ends, we run each team's latest submission that passed review once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. It is similar, not the same: the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different websites (other software, layout, navigation and site names), other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle them as it finds them. That run weighs most when we pick the winners, so don't tune your agent to the public scenario.

## Bid rules

The brief states these rules in full. Together they define exactly one correct answer.

1. **Quantity:** The tender quantity, overridden by the latest clarification that changes that position.
2. **Requirement:** The position's requirement in the specification revision marked current.
3. **Material:** The active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification match exactly. If a position has none, the answer is no bid.
4. **Unit price:** The price condition valid on the scenario date, at the highest quantity scale reached, minus the approved discount, rounded half-up to the cent.
5. **Discount:** The most recent approval from the sales director for this exact tender; otherwise 0 %.
6. **Lead time:** The from-stock lead time when stock covers the quantity, otherwise the production lead time.
7. **Total:** The sum of quantity times unit price, rounded half-up to the cent.
8. **Decision:** Bid, with one entry per tender position; no bid with no positions and a total of 0 when a material is missing.
9. **Partial submission:** Full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
10. **Finding records:** The specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes. Empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue; narrow to at most 20 results. Mail search combines words with AND: use the tender reference plus a subject/topic. Read the appropriate inbox/archive results. Opened pages and selected result sets may be extracted by helpers. Sites and positions can be investigated in parallel; no shared request quota or mandatory site order applies.
11. **Agent requirement:** A language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
12. **Commercial clauses:** A tender Q&A answer may assign a position to a Konditionsgruppe. Resolve that key in the latest Konditionsregeln message for the exact reference from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. Its prose determines whether discount applies to base only, base plus mass surcharge, or neither; setup fees are always excluded. A group overrides the default rule, even when two positions select the same material. The separately reported surcharge is always BEFORE any discount. Positions without a group use the default base-only rule. The order-level approved percentage and its threshold calculation do not change.
13. **Withdrawn answers:** A tender Q&A answer may withdraw (zurückziehen) an earlier answer by its number. Ignore the withdrawn answer's quantity change; the latest remaining change applies, otherwise the tender quantity.
14. **Scoped amendments:** After selecting the governing full specification revision, read the tender Q&A for technical amendments naming that revision and requirement. Apply only the named attributes; all others are inherited. The latest dated applicable amendment wins per attribute. Amendments to other revisions do not apply.
15. **Shared stock:** Sum final quantities of all positions selecting the same material. Stock must cover that entire sum for every such position to use stock delivery; otherwise all use production delivery. No partial stock allocation. Price scales remain per position, not per material sum.
16. **Conditional discount:** The latest exact-reference director approval may require a minimum undiscounted net order value. Compute that value from final quantities and valid per-position scale prices before any discount and excluding mass surcharges and setup fees, rounded half up to cents. The threshold is inclusive. If it fails, use 0 %, without falling back to older approvals. For no_bid a conditional approval yields 0 %.
17. **Units:** Tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
18. **Pricing breakdown:** Base_unit_price, surcharge_per_unit, packaging_per_unit and rebate_total are optional and earn independent credit. All monetary answers are net EUR. Base, surcharge and packaging are per piece; rebate_total is the credit for the whole position. Enter 0.00 for a known zero; blank means unanswered. Do not feed rounded per-piece breakdowns back into the final formula.
19. These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets. Missing calculation fields lose only their own points; signing an incomplete bid is supported.
20. **Technical derivation:** For a requirement marked nutzbarer Weg, apply its scoped amendments first, then add twice the per-end reserve from the revision-specific Technikfreigabe. Match the resulting nominal stroke to the ERP. Do not change the other attributes.
21. **Authority and time:** Resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
22. **Currency:** The valid condition names its currency and FX key. Normalize its price unit, select the per-position quantity scale, then convert with EUR per currency unit and HALF_UP to cents. This converted base_unit_price is used in all subsequent calculations and approval thresholds.
23. **Packaging:** Q&A assigns the tariff key; ERP gives pieces per carton. Charge ceil(final pieces / carton size) cartons independently per position. Do not increase the bid quantity. Report packaging_per_unit in EUR, rounded HALF_UP; do not discount packaging.
24. **Delivery:** Q&A assigns a commitment key. Apply it only if its material matches and pooled final demand for that material is within its inclusive ceiling. Otherwise use shared-stock delivery. A commitment may differ by position even for the same material.
25. **Shared setup:** Q&A identifies pool members; ERP gives allocation mass (distinct from surcharge mass); the Rüstpools mail gives the one pool fee. Allocate by quantity × allocation mass using the cent-allocation rule in that mail. Add each allocation to that position's ordinary setup fee. Report surcharge_per_unit BEFORE discount, excluding packaging and bonus.
26. **Project bonus:** The finance mail gives marginal percentage bands. Compute the eligible undiscounted EUR goods total, apply each band only to its portion, round the aggregate credit HALF_UP to cents, then allocate proportionally to eligible line goods values using largest remainders in cents (ties: ascending position identifier). Report rebate_total as the allocated EUR CREDIT FOR THE ENTIRE POSITION, not per piece; enter zero for nonmembers. This bonus is independent of discount clauses.
27. **Final price:** Clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
28. **Metal indices:** Select the latest exact-reference Preisindizes message from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. If the code lists validity windows, use the rate whose inclusive window contains the scenario date, not the last rate listed.
29. **Scoring in bid cases:** Decision 5, reference 5, discount 5, positions 75 minus any additional checks, correct total 5, arithmetic consistency 5. When present, the withdrawn Q&A quantity and date-selected metal-index checks earn 5 points each. Within each equally weighted position: material 20%, quantity 15%, base price 15%, surcharge 10%, packaging 10%, project bonus 10%, final unit price 10%, delivery 10%. Each field is independent; optional breakdown fields can be blank. No-bid scoring is unchanged.

## How a run works

Develop on your machine against the public websites with the scouting logins (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox: `atira test-run` uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live, or drop the package on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). A test run lasts up to 2 hours on the public data and returns its score with the full breakdown. In the commands, `$ATIRA_TOKEN` holds your personal token (sign in with `atira login`, then `atira token`).

1. **Start.** The run issues a token, the task brief and fresh logins for every website.
2. **Read.** Your agent reads the brief, the rules and the answer format from the API.
3. **Work the websites.** It works through the 4 websites in a real browser and gathers the facts.
4. **Submit.** It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.
5. **Scored.** The answer is checked against the one correct answer; quality, cost and time are recorded.

### Develop locally

```sh
eval "$(atira scout --challenge rfq --env)"   # logins for the public websites
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting"   # the same, with the brief, as JSON
# run your agent on your machine, then once in the sandbox:
atira test-run ./my-agent --challenge rfq
```

`atira scout --env` exports the scouting logins as `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the shape a run gets), each website's URL, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the brief and the answer format. It also points the free hosted models at `atira models proxy` on your computer, so your agent needs no model key; another provider takes your own. Nothing done there counts. With these logins, an answer entered on the tender portal is acknowledged but never counts. In a run, your agent reads the same at `GET /v1/runs/current` with the run token as `x-api-key`, and hands in one valid answer of up to 65,536 bytes; a malformed one returns its problems while the clock keeps running.

### Read the run

Inside a test or scored run, with the run token (`$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`) in `RUN_TOKEN`:

```sh
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/runs/current" -H "x-api-key: $RUN_TOKEN"
```

The response holds `brief` (the task in Markdown, with the rules), `access` (each website's `url` and `credentials`), `submission` (where the answer goes), `answer_schema`, `expires_at`, `llm_proxy_url` and `llm_providers`. Outside a run, `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` returns the brief, logins, answer target and schema for the public websites, without a token.

### In the sandbox

A test run and a scored run start your `run` command with these variables. `setup` runs before, with network but without them, for up to 5 minutes that don't count toward your time.

| `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: one per browser asked for in agent.json, up to 4 |
| `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started, 1 to 4 |
| `DISPLAY` | the desktop browser 1 runs on, :1 at 1280×800; browser n is on :n |
| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `http_proxy`, `https_proxy` | the only way out: the platform and the websites (http://127.0.0.1:3128) |
| `NO_PROXY`, `no_proxy` | reached directly, so the browser's CDP stays local (localhost,127.0.0.1) |
| `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY` | Node's fetch uses the proxy (1) |

Every model call goes through the platform's metering proxy, which records its tokens and cost; the hosted models need no key, and any other provider takes the team's own. [The run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls) has the key and SDK settings for each provider.

## Unlimited Inference

We host Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare's Clef for this hackathon, free and with no usage cap. On your laptop, `atira models proxy` gives you a URL and key (setup on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team#team-models)). In test and scored runs it's set up for you. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair.

### Qwen3.8-Flash-Next

#6 on the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/qwen3-8-flash-next) (open-weight, large models). Multimodal general-purpose LLM. Strong at reasoning, tool calls and reading pages and screenshots, with a 256k context, so it can plan, browse and write the answer.

- **Limits:** No usage cap. Up to 32 calls per team at once, across all its runs; more wait in line.
- **Simulated pricing:**
  - Input: $0.15 / M tokens
  - Cached input: $0.016 / M tokens
  - Cache writes: Free
  - Output: $0.47 / M tokens
- **Precision:** [NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4) (NVIDIA's checkpoint)

Scales to zero when idle, but warm-up isn't counted toward a submission's time.

```python
import os
from openai import OpenAI

qwen = OpenAI(
    base_url=os.environ["QWEN_BASE_URL"],
    api_key=os.environ["QWEN_API_KEY"],
)
reply = qwen.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen",
    messages=[{
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Which button submits?",
    }],
)
```

### Cloudflare Clef

A multimodal decision model. Give it a state and up to 4 screenshots, then ask it questions: `choice` picks one of your options, `noul` gives the probability of yes, from 0 to 1, and `score` rates on a scale you set. See [Cloudflare's announcement](https://blog.cloudflare.com/clef-decision-models/) and [the benchmarks](https://clef-evals.workers-ai-mle.workers.dev). Worth a try for quick, low-stakes decisions, such as which link to open or whether a page is the right document, while the bigger model reads and reasons.

- **Limits:** No usage cap. Up to 16 calls per team at once, across all its runs; more wait in line.
- **Simulated pricing:**
  - Input: $0.24 / M tokens
  - Output: Not priced

Scales to zero when idle, but warm-up isn't counted toward a submission's time.

```sh
curl "$CLEF_BASE_URL/v1/decide" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLEF_API_KEY" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "state": {"page": "Checkout returns 502"},
  "questions": {"next": {
    "type": "choice",
    "instructions": "What next?",
    "criteria": {
      "retry": "Retry the request",
      "report": "Report the error"}}}}'
```

In a run, `QWEN_BASE_URL` with `QWEN_API_KEY` and `CLEF_BASE_URL` with `CLEF_API_KEY` are set for you. On your machine, `atira models proxy` serves the same APIs on 127.0.0.1, so the same code works in both. Calls from your machine are free, recorded and never ranked. An idle model can take several minutes to wake on its first call, so use long timeouts.

```sh
atira login   # once per computer
atira models proxy   # keep it running; it prints:
export QWEN_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8765/qwen/v1
export QWEN_API_KEY=local
export CLEF_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8765/clef
export CLEF_API_KEY=local
```

Cost and time count toward your rank, and a call to these models costs a fraction of a frontier call. Use them for the easy steps.

If one fails mid-run, retry the call, as with any provider. If they were down for most of a run that then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count, and a scored run starts again once by itself.

## Submitting

A submission is your agent as a gzipped tarball. It is reviewed automatically, then run once in the sandbox on the public dataset, and that score ranks your team. Submit as often as you like, one at a time; your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard, and your latest one that passed review goes into the final run.

### agent.json

```json
{
  "setup": ["uv", "sync"],
  "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"],
  "models": ["qwen"]
}
```

Put `agent.json` at the root of the tarball, next to your code and its dependency file. Up to 20 MB compressed. `setup` installs dependencies with network access, within 5 minutes that don't count toward your time; `run` is timed and reaches only the platform and the websites. `"browsers": 1–4` (default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts, each on its own screen. `"models"` lists the hosted models your agent calls; the run waits only for those to warm up (for all of them when it's absent). Node 24 with pnpm and bun, Python 3.12 with uv, and Rust with cargo are installed. The [starter kit](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal skeleton to start from.

### Upload

```sh
tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
  "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions"
```

Or drop the tarball on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). Upload it as a test run first to watch it work in the sandbox: its browser live, its logs, and a recording afterwards.

### Test run first

The same tarball as a test run: one run in the scored-run sandbox on the public data, with live browser frames, logs and a recording.

```sh
tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
  "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/rehearsals"
```

### Follow your submissions

```sh
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions" -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN"
```

Logs of test runs and scored runs, from a cursor (`after`); repeat with the returned `cursor` until `chunks` is empty:

```sh
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/runs/$RUN_ID/logs?after=0" -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN"
```

## Scoring and ranking

Every submission is measured on its run in the sandbox.

- **Quality:** 0 to 100. Every field of the bid is compared with the one correct answer: tender reference, positions, materials, quantities, unit prices, lead times, discount and total, each position's base price and surcharge per piece, packaging, allocated project bonus, and whether the total adds up.
- **Eligibility:** The right tender reference; a wrong decision loses quality points but other correct fields keep their credit. A bid that is not eligible ranks after every eligible one.
- **Cost:** Every model call goes through the proxy and is priced per model. There is no budget: at equal quality, cost × time decides.
- **Time:** Wall-clock time from the start of the run until the answer is accepted. It weighs as much as cost: halving either halves cost × time.

Order: Eligible first → Quality ↓ → Cost × time ↑.

Eligible answers rank first, then higher quality. At equal quality, the lower product of cost and time wins, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time as at least 1 s, so among free runs the faster one wins.

## Fair play

Your agent has to find the answer itself.

- Your system must work the answer out from the websites at run time, with a model doing the navigating and deciding. A coding agent reviews every package; hardcoded answers, fixed scripts and crawlers are rejected.
- Bring your own model key for Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google, Groq, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI, Together, Fireworks, kept as a team secret. Every call goes through the run's proxy and is metered at the published prices. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare Clef are ours, unlimited. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair. The sandbox reaches the platform and the websites, nothing else.
- At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up to 4 in agent.json ("browsers"), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The sandbox stops any other browser your agent starts.
- One submission in flight per team. Submit again once it has finished.

Rules at a glance: [Fair play](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md)

# From RFQ to bid

**Turn a public tender into a correct, signed bid without a person touching it.**

You work for a German hydraulics manufacturer that wants to bid on a public tender for hydraulic cylinders. What you need is spread over four websites: the tender portal, a supplier portal with the buyer's specification, your company's ERP and the sales inbox. They behave like real business software, with logins, popups, session timeouts and outdated documents. Your agent reads all of it, applies the bid rules and enters one priced, signed bid in the tender portal.

**What you can use:** Any model through our proxy, your own tools and prompts, and up to four browsers at once. A model does the work in the sandbox: it finds its way through the websites and makes the decisions during the run. No fixed scripts, no crawlers, no copied values, no person helping.

**How you win:** Your bid has to be eligible first. After that, the most accurate bid wins, and between equally accurate bids, the cheaper and faster one. The leaderboard uses the public data. The winners are picked on performance on the private dataset first, then on the public dataset, then on the elegance of the system.

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Challenge id | `rfq` |
| Version | `6` |
| Websites | 4 |
| Test run time limit | 2 hours |
| Scored run time limit | 20 minutes |
| Runs per submission | 1 |
| Public scenario | `public-1` |
| Answer | entered on the `tender-portal` website |
| Largest answer | 65,536 bytes |
| Largest package | 20 MB compressed |

Web page: [https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq) · Leaderboard: [Markdown](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md) · Getting started: [Markdown](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/start.md) · For agents: [llms.txt](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/llms.txt) · [OpenAPI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/openapi.json) · [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md) · [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md)

## Quick start for agents

Set the platform URL, install the CLI and sign in once: `atira login` opens the browser, where you approve a personal token for this device (`atira login --device` prints a link and a code instead, for a machine without a browser; plain curl uses the [device flow](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#signing-in)). Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header, or as `Authorization: Bearer`.

```sh
export ATIRA_API=https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai
curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | sh   # the CLI for Node 24; read it first: curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | less
# or without installing: curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/cli.mjs" -o atira.mjs && node atira.mjs --help
atira login   # approve in the browser
export ATIRA_TOKEN=$(atira token)   # for curl
eval "$(atira scout --challenge rfq --env)"   # logins for the public websites, to run your agent locally
atira test-run ./my-agent --challenge rfq   # one sandbox run on the public dataset, opened live
atira submit ./my-agent --challenge rfq     # review, then the scored run on the public dataset
atira status
```

## The task

One tender, four German websites, one bid.

The agent produces: **One bid**. It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.

## The websites

Each run gets its own logins, in the run's `access`. To look around yourself, use the scouting logins below. Expect what real business software throws at you: popups, session timeouts, outdated documents and look-alike records. Everything your agent needs fits on a 1280×800 screen.

### 1. Tender portal (Vergabeportal, `tender-portal`)
